titleBlock.headline: Rapamycin fed late in life extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice
titleBlock.authors: Harrison, D.E., Strong, R., Sharp, Z.D., Nelson, J.F., Astle, C.M., Flurkey, K., Nadon, N.L., Wilkinson, J.E., Frenkel, K., Carter, C.S., Pahor, M., Javors, M.A., Fernandez, E., Miller, R.A.

researchSummary:
This is a summary of the scientific study.
Not affiliated with the study authors or their institutions.
whatIsMtor: The mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) is an evolutionarily conserved serine/threonine kinase that integrates amino acid, insulin/IGF-1, and energy signals. It operates in two distinct complexes: mTORC1 (which drives protein translation via S6K1/4E-BP1 and suppresses ULK1/TFEB autophagy) and mTORC2 (which regulates Akt survival and glucose/lipid homeostasis).
The Anabolic Growth vs. Autophagic Repair Seesaw

When nutrients and amino acids (especially leucine) are abundant, mTORC1 turns ON to drive cellular hypertrophy and division while blocking recycling. When nutrients are scarce—or when rapamycin allosterically binds FKBP12 to inhibit mTORC1—cells switch into deep autophagic clearance and proteostatic maintenance.
What did this NIA ITP study discover?

Due to formulation delays, microencapsulated rapamycin (14 ppm in chow) was not started until mice were already 600 days old (~60 human years). Remarkably, late-life treatment extended remaining life expectancy from 600 days by +38% in females and +28% in males, and increased overall maximum lifespan (90th percentile) by +14% in females and +9% in males across all three independent test sites.

studyOverview.label: Objective
studyOverview.value: Test whether pharmacological mTORC1 inhibition extends mammalian lifespan across three independent NIA Interventions Testing Program (ITP) laboratories.

studyOverview.label: The Intervention
studyOverview.value: Enteric-coated microencapsulated Rapamycin (eRapa, 14 ppm) initiated at 600 days of age (~60 human years) in n = 1,901 UM-HET3 mice.

studyOverview.label: Remaining Life Expectancy
studyOverview.value: +38% in females (from 600 days) and +28% in males (comparable to late-life D+Q senolytics at +36%).

studyOverview.label: Maximum Lifespan (90th Pct)
studyOverview.value: +14% in females (1,094 -> 1,245 days) and +9% in males (1,078 -> 1,179 days), replicated at all 3 sites.

scorecardOverview.title: The Question
scorecardOverview.content: Can a pharmacological small molecule initiated late in middle age (600 days, equivalent to ~60 human years) reproducibly extend both median and maximum lifespan in genetically diverse mammals?

scorecardOverview.title: The Methodology
scorecardOverview.content: Evaluated microencapsulated rapamycin (14 ppm in food) across 1,901 genetically heterogeneous UM-HET3 mice tested simultaneously at three independent NIA ITP laboratories (Jackson Lab, Univ. of Michigan, UT Health San Antonio).

scorecardOverview.title: The Breakthrough
scorecardOverview.content: Late-life rapamycin increased remaining life expectancy after 600 days by +38% in females and +28% in males, and raised overall maximum lifespan (90th percentile age) by +14% in females and +9% in males.

mechanismDescription: Rapamycin forms a gain-of-function complex with intracellular FKBP12 that allosterically inhibits mTORC1 (lowering ribosomal S6 phosphorylation), releasing the brake on ULK1/TFEB-driven macroautophagy, clearing damaged organelles, preserving stem cell quiescence, and delaying neoplasia.

keyFindings.title: Late-Life Efficacy (Started at 600 Days)
keyFindings.desc: Initiating rapamycin at 600 days of age (~60 human years) still captured the majority of the longevity benefit—extending remaining life expectancy by 38% in females and 28% in males.

keyFindings.title: True Maximum Lifespan Extension
keyFindings.desc: Evaluating the 90th percentile survival age (Wang/Allison test), rapamycin increased overall maximum lifespan from 1,094 to 1,245 days (+14%) in females and from 1,078 to 1,179 days (+9%) in males (p < 0.0001).

keyFindings.title: Gold-Standard 3-Site Reproducibility
keyFindings.desc: Statistically significant survival extension was independently achieved in both sexes at all three NIA ITP centers (TJL, UM, UTHSCSA) in genetically heterogeneous four-way cross (UM-HET3) mice.

keyFindings.title: mTORC1 vs. mTORC2 Selectivity
keyFindings.desc: Follow-up work showed that rapamycin's longevity benefits come from acute mTORC1 inhibition, whereas chronic unpulsed exposure secondarily disrupts mTORC2 (causing insulin resistance and dyslipidemia).

conclusions: Pharmacological inhibition of mTORC1 extends both median and maximum lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mammals, even when started at 600 days of age.
Measured from treatment onset (600 days), rapamycin extends remaining life expectancy by +38% (females) and +28% (males)—providing a direct benchmark for late-life interventions.
Distinguishing mTORC1 restraint (autophagy/longevity) from chronic mTORC2 disruption underpins modern intermittent dosing protocols.

structuredConclusions.title: Late-Life Plasticity of Mammalian Aging
structuredConclusions.content: Starting rapamycin at 600 days (~60 human years) extended remaining life expectancy by 38% in females and 28% in males, overturning the dogma that geroprotectors must be started in youth.

structuredConclusions.title: Multi-Site Genetic Heterogeneity Proof
structuredConclusions.content: Tested across 1,901 genetically diverse UM-HET3 mice at three independent NIA ITP laboratories, rapamycin extended overall 90th-percentile maximum lifespan by +14% (females) and +9% (males).

structuredConclusions.title: Pulsed mTORC1 Selectivity in Translation
structuredConclusions.content: Because acute rapamycin inhibits mTORC1 while chronic daily exposure disrupts mTORC2, human clinical translation (e.g., Mannick et al., 2014/2018; PEARL trial) utilizes intermittent weekly dosing to enhance immune and autophagic function.

protocolRecommendations: Sirolimus (Rapamycin) is a prescription-only FDA-approved medication; human longevity trials (such as Mannick et al. with low-dose/intermittent mTOR inhibition and the PEARL trial) investigate weekly pulsed regimens to target mTORC1 while sparing mTORC2.

Notice the metric distinction when comparing papers: Rapamycin's +14% (F) / +9% (M) figure is total lifespan from birth, whereas its remaining life expectancy from treatment onset at 600 days is +38% (F) / +28% (M) (directly comparable to D+Q's +36% post-treatment survival).

Physiological protocols that transiently suppress mTORC1 and activate AMPK/ULK1 autophagy—including periodic fasting, caloric moderation (Fiorito et al., 2025), and endurance exercise—engage the same nutrient-sensing switch without pharmacological immunosuppression.
